items.stem: In the 1930s the scholars Milman Parry and Albert Lord recorded hundreds of heroic songs performed by folk singers in Yugoslavia, most of whom could not read or write. One of these singers, Avdo Međedović, performed for them a song of more than 12,000 lines. Parry and Lord found that the singers do not memorize a fixed text. In each performance a singer builds the song anew from a stock of traditional phrases and scenes that he learned from older singers, and Lord recorded the same singer performing the same song several times, with differences in length and in details. Based on the text, a song performed by such a singer -
options: is learned word for word from an older singer, and changes only when the singer forgets part of it
receives its final form the first time the singer performs it, and all his later performances repeat that form
is the singer's own invention and does not rely on material used by other singers
is put together anew each time from traditional material, so that no two performances of it are exactly alike
items.explanation: The singers rebuild the song in every performance from inherited phrases, and the same song came out differently each time. (2) fixes the song at its first performance, (1) makes it memorized, and (3) denies the traditional stock.
items.he_draft: בשנות השלושים הקליטו החוקרים מילמן פרי ואלברט לורד מאות שירי גבורה שביצעו זמרים עממיים ביוגוסלביה, שרובם לא ידעו קרוא וכתוב. אחד מהם, אבדו מדג'דוביץ', ביצע בפניהם שיר של יותר מ-12,000 שורות. החוקרים מצאו שהזמרים אינם משננים טקסט קבוע: בכל ביצוע הם מרכיבים את השיר מחדש מתוך מאגר של צירופים מסורתיים... על סמך הטקסט, שיר שזמר כזה מבצע -
facts: Milman Parry and Albert Lord recorded South Slavic oral epic singers (guslars) in Yugoslavia in the 1930s
Most singers were illiterate
Avdo Međedović dictated/performed 'The Wedding of Smailagić Meho', over 12,000 lines
They found oral-formulaic composition: songs recomposed in performance from traditional formulas and themes; performances of the same song vary (Lord, The Singer of Tales, 1960)

items.stem: According to the principle of competitive exclusion, when several species compete for the same limited resources in a uniform environment, in the end only a few of them survive, because the species that uses a given resource most efficiently pushes out the others. The ecologist G. Evelyn Hutchinson pointed out that the phytoplankton of lakes and seas does not seem to obey this principle. The water in which these tiny algae live is relatively uniform, and they all depend on a small number of resources - light and a few minerals - yet dozens of species live side by side in the same body of water. Hutchinson called this "the paradox of the plankton". According to the text, why is the situation of the plankton paradoxical?
options: Because all the species of plankton compete for the same resources, and yet none of them has an advantage over the others
Because the number of plankton species in a lake is larger than the number of resources, even though each species needs more than one resource
Because in an environment like theirs only a few species would be expected to survive, and yet many species live together
Because according to the principle of competitive exclusion, species that compete cannot live in the same lake, and yet plankton species are found in many different lakes
items.explanation: The principle predicts few survivors in a uniform environment with few resources; the plankton shows many. (1) adds a claim the text does not make, (2) invents a comparison, and (4) misreads the principle as being about different lakes.
items.he_draft: האקולוג ג' אוולין האצ'ינסון כינה זאת "הפרדוקס של הפלנקטון"...
facts: Competitive exclusion principle (Gause): species competing for the same limiting resources cannot stably coexist
G. Evelyn Hutchinson, 'The Paradox of the Plankton', American Naturalist, 1961
Phytoplankton live in relatively homogeneous water, compete for light and few nutrients, yet many species coexist

items.stem: The bar-tailed godwit, a wading bird that normally weighs only a few hundred grams, flies every autumn from Alaska to New Zealand, a distance of more than 11,000 kilometers, without landing even once; the flight lasts eight or nine days. Before setting out, the birds eat so much that their weight almost doubles, and most of the added weight is fat, which serves as fuel. At the same time, some of their digestive organs, which are not needed during the flight, shrink considerably, so that the birds carry less weight. The godwits also do not leave on just any day: they wait for winds that blow in the direction of their flight. Which of the following is not given in the text as something that helps the godwits complete their flight?
options: During the flight they sleep with half of the brain at a time
They store a large amount of fat in their bodies
Organs that they do not need during the flight become considerably smaller
They set out when the wind will blow in their favor
items.explanation: Sleep during the flight is not mentioned at all. (2), (3) and (4) are the fat, the shrinking organs and the waiting for favorable winds.
facts: Bar-tailed godwits (Limosa lapponica baueri) fly nonstop from Alaska to New Zealand, about 11,000-12,000 km, in roughly 8-9 days
They weigh a few hundred grams and nearly double their mass with fat before departure
Digestive organs (gizzard, intestine, liver) shrink before migration
They time departure with favorable winds

items.stem: Experts at a museum in the country of Vessaria are examining a small drawing of a harbor signed with the initials M.R. It may be an early work by the painter Matthias Roven, whose later paintings of harbors are among the best known in the country. Tests of the paper show that it was probably made in the northern provinces, where Roven lived until the age of thirty, although dozens of other artists in the north used the same kind of paper. It is known that as long as Roven lived in the north he drew only on local paper. The experts are of the opinion that if the drawing is Roven's, it dates from his years in the north. Which of the following claims can be inferred from the text?
options: If the paper was not made in the north, the drawing is probably not by one of the northern artists but by Roven
The chance that Roven made the drawing while he lived in the north is not greater than the chance that the paper was made in the north
If the paper was made in the north, it is likely that the drawing is by Roven
The chance that Roven made the drawing after he left the north is greater than the chance that he made it while he still lived there
items.explanation: A drawing by Roven from his northern years must be on northern paper, so that possibility cannot be more likely than northern paper. (3) reverses the condition, since many artists used the paper, (1) points the wrong way, and (4) contradicts the experts.
items.he_draft: חוקרים במוזיאון בארץ מסוימת בודקים רישום...

items.stem: The Phaistos Disc, a clay disc about 16 centimeters in diameter that was found in 1908 in the palace of Phaistos in southern Crete, is covered on both sides with 241 signs arranged in a spiral. The signs were pressed into the wet clay with stamps before the disc was fired, and for this reason some have called it the earliest example of printing. Most scholars believe that the signs record a language, but if so, the text is too short for it to be deciphered with any certainty. A few scholars have even suggested that the disc is a forgery made at the time of its discovery. Which of the following is presented in the text as a fact?
options: The signs on the disc record a language
The disc was made at the time of its discovery
The signs were made in the clay with stamps
The disc is the earliest example of printing
items.explanation: Only the method by which the signs were made is stated without qualification. (1) is what most scholars believe, (2) is what a few suggest, and (4) is what some have called it.
facts: The Phaistos Disc was found in 1908 (Luigi Pernier) in the Minoan palace of Phaistos, Crete
About 16 cm diameter, 241 (sometimes counted 242) stamped signs in a spiral on both sides, impressed before firing
Often described as the earliest example of movable-type printing
Undeciphered; too short for secure decipherment; a forgery hypothesis has been raised (e.g. Eisenberg 2008)

items.stem: In a study carried out in 2010 in a hotel room in Indianapolis, 21 experienced violinists played on six violins - three new ones and three made about three hundred years ago by Stradivari and Guarneri - while wearing dark goggles, so that they could not tell which instrument was which. Most of them could not tell the old violins from the new ones, and the violin chosen most often as the best was a new one. A violin dealer who was asked about the study said: "I do not dispute the results. Under these conditions, in a small room, perhaps no one can hear the difference. But a violin is bought in order to be played in a concert hall, before an audience, and this study tells us nothing about that." What is the dealer's position on the study?
options: Its results are doubtful, since the violinists could not see which violin they were playing
Its results may be correct, but they do not answer the question that matters to those who buy violins
It shows that there is no difference between old and new violins either in a small room or in a concert hall
It is mistaken, since in a small room the difference between the violins is easier to hear than in a concert hall
items.explanation: The dealer accepts the results for the conditions of the study and denies that they bear on the concert hall. (1) and (4) dispute results he accepts, and (3) extends the results to the hall, which is exactly what he rejects.
items.he_draft: במחקר שנערך ב-2010... סוחר כינורות אמר...
facts: Fritz et al., PNAS 2012: double-blind test in a hotel room in Indianapolis (2010 International Violin Competition)
21 violinists, 6 violins: 3 new, 2 Stradivari, 1 Guarneri del Gesù; welders' goggles
Players could not reliably tell old from new; the most-preferred violin was new (and the least-preferred was a Stradivari)
The dealer's remark is an invented, unnamed reaction

items.stem: Oaks, beeches and a number of other trees do not produce the same quantity of seeds every year. In most years they produce few seeds, and once every few years they produce an enormous quantity. This phenomenon is called "masting", and its most striking feature is that it is synchronized: the trees of the same species over a large area produce a large crop in the same years. One explanation is that in the years of plenty the animals that eat the seeds cannot eat them all, so that many seeds remain and can sprout. Which of the following describes masting?
options: A certain beech tree produced many seeds every year, whereas the beeches around it produced few
In a certain forest each oak produced a large crop of acorns once every few years, but not all the oaks in the same year
All the oaks in a certain forest produced a moderate number of acorns every year
In one year all the beeches in a large forest produced a great many seeds, and in the next three years almost none
items.explanation: Masting requires both a large crop only in some years and synchronization among the trees. (2) has the first without the second, (1) has neither, and (3) has no variation at all.
facts: Masting: highly variable, synchronized seed production among individuals of a population (oaks, beeches and others)
Predator satiation hypothesis (Janzen 1971; Silvertown 1980): seed predators cannot consume all seeds in mast years

items.stem: In the Niassa reserve in Mozambique, honey hunters of the Yao people are led to wild bees' nests by a small bird, the greater honeyguide, and in return the bird eats the wax that is left after they take the honey. When they look for honey, the hunters make a special call, a trill followed by a grunt. In a study published in 2016, researchers played recordings of this call and of other sounds and found that the call roughly doubled the chance that a honeyguide would guide them. The researchers suggested that the birds learn to recognize the call, but the study itself did not show this. Which of the following headlines best suits a report on the study?
options: Honeyguides in Mozambique respond to the call of the honey hunters. Do they learn it?
Birds understand the language of the Yao: honeyguides learn the hunters' call
The honeyguides of all Africa answer the same human call
A special call doubles the amount of honey that the Yao collect
items.explanation: The study showed a response to the call; learning is only suspected. (2) states the learning as proven, (3) extends the finding to all of Africa, and (4) confuses the chance of being guided with the amount of honey.
facts: Spottiswoode, Begg & Begg, Science, 2016: Yao honey hunters in the Niassa National Reserve, Mozambique
The hunters use a 'brrr-hm' call (trill followed by grunt)
Playback of the call raised the probability of being guided from about 33% to 66% compared with control sounds
Honeyguides eat the wax; the authors suggested the response is learned (later work, 2023, on Hadza whistles supported local learning)

items.stem: Hila: "When a doctor treats a member of his own family, he knows the patient's history and habits better than any other doctor could. He also knows which questions the patient will avoid answering and how he reacts to pain. But it is precisely this closeness that makes it hard for the doctor to tell the patient bad news, and to insist on tests that the patient does not want." Which of the following claims is implied by Hila's words?
options: A doctor who treats a member of his family usually hides bad news from the patient
Another doctor would know less about the patient, and would therefore be more willing to tell him bad news
The closeness between a doctor and a relative helps the treatment more than it harms it
What a doctor knows about a relative's condition is not necessarily what he will manage to tell him
items.explanation: The same closeness gives the doctor knowledge and makes some of it hard to share. (1) turns difficulty into habit, (2) adds a "therefore" Hila does not state, and (3) weighs advantages that she does not weigh.

items.stem: Some historians have seen the medieval peasant who prayed for rain and at the same time dug irrigation channels as a person who did not distinguish between religion and practical knowledge. Other historians reject this view. In their opinion, peasants knew perfectly well that a channel brings water to a field, and many villages invested years of labor in their channels. However, they also knew that even fields that were well watered sometimes failed, because of hail, disease or pests, and that no one could predict such disasters. According to the second group of historians, what did the peasants believe?
options: In dry years prayer could take the place of digging channels
Religion and practical knowledge serve the same purpose, and there is therefore no reason to distinguish between them
Practical work could improve the harvest, but it could not guarantee it
Fields that were well watered failed only in villages that did not pray for rain
items.explanation: On this view the peasants dug because digging works, and prayed because it is not enough. (1) drops the practical work, (2) is the first group's view, and (4) invents a cause the peasants themselves could not predict.

items.stem: Norvelia has only two universities, one in the capital, Aster, and one in the port city of Lenn. Over the past decade the number of candidates for the faculties of medicine and of law has risen at both of them, although the total number of students in the country has hardly changed. At the University of Aster the number of candidates for medicine has risen at a faster rate than the number of candidates for law, whereas at the University of Lenn the number of candidates for law has risen at a faster rate than the number of candidates for medicine. Which of the following claims can be inferred from the text?
options: At the University of Aster there are more candidates for medicine than for law
At the University of Lenn the number of candidates for medicine has risen more slowly than the number of candidates for law
The number of candidates for medicine has risen at a faster rate at the University of Aster than at the University of Lenn
At the University of Lenn only the number of candidates for law has risen, while the total number of students has not changed
items.explanation: The text compares rates only within each university. (1) confuses a rate with a number, (3) compares the two universities, and (4) denies the rise in medicine at Lenn.
items.he_draft: בעשור האחרון עלה מספר המועמדים לרפואה ולמשפטים בשתי האוניברסיטאות של נורבליה...

items.stem: Jewish custom forbids destroying worn-out writings that may contain the name of God, and they are therefore placed in a storeroom called a geniza. The Jews of Fustat, the old city of Cairo, placed in the geniza of the Ben Ezra Synagogue not only prayer books but also letters, contracts, bills, shopping lists and children's exercises, and the dry climate preserved them for about a thousand years. The fragments number in the hundreds of thousands, and at the end of the nineteenth century Solomon Schechter took the largest collection of them to Cambridge. From them the historian S. D. Goitein reconstructed in great detail the daily life, trade and family relations of the Jews of the Mediterranean in the Middle Ages. What is the main subject of the text?
options: The reasons why Jewish custom forbids destroying worn-out writings
Solomon Schechter's work at Cambridge at the end of the nineteenth century
The history of the Jews of Cairo in the Middle Ages
The Cairo Geniza as a source of knowledge about everyday life
items.explanation: The text explains why the geniza holds ordinary documents and what historians learned from them. (1) and (2) are single stages of that story, and (3) is what the documents reveal, not what the text is about.
items.he_draft: הגניזה של בית הכנסת בן עזרא בפוסטאט...
facts: A geniza stores worn-out texts that may contain God's name rather than destroying them
The Ben Ezra Synagogue geniza in Fustat (Old Cairo) held letters, contracts, accounts, etc., preserved by the dry climate over about a millennium
Solomon Schechter brought most of it to Cambridge in 1896-97; fragments number roughly 300,000-400,000
S. D. Goitein, A Mediterranean Society, reconstructed daily life of medieval Mediterranean Jews

items.stem: Nili: "The city should restore the old cinema building on the main square and turn it into a cultural center. The building is part of the history of the city, and residents of every age have memories connected with it." Eldad: "Restoring the cinema would cost almost three times as much as putting up a new building, and its hall is too small for concerts. The building has no special value. If the city wants a cultural center, it should build one near the train station, where there is room for parking." With which of the following claims would both Nili and Eldad agree?
options: The old cinema building is not suited to be a cultural center
It would be good for the city to have a cultural center
The old cinema building is part of the history of the city
A cultural center should be built near the train station
items.explanation: Nili wants the center in the cinema, Eldad near the station, but both want a center. (1) and (4) are Eldad's claims only, and (3) is Nili's, which Eldad denies.
items.he_draft: נילי ואלדד על בניין הקולנוע הישן

items.stem: The following is from the introduction to an atlas of the dialects of a certain country: "The maps in this atlas divide the country into dialect regions by means of clear lines. We do not claim that the speech of the residents changes at these lines: in most places it changes gradually from one village to the next, and two neighboring villages on either side of a line may speak almost alike. However, without such lines the reader could not compare the regions with one another, and a map that tried to show every gradual change would be impossible to read." Which of the following best expresses the position of the atlas's authors?
options: The lines on the maps do not reflect the way in which speech changes, but they are necessary in order to compare the regions
Since speech changes gradually, it is not possible to divide the country into dialect regions
The lines show the places at which the speech of the residents changes most sharply
A good dialect map should show every gradual change in the speech of the residents, even if it is hard to read
items.explanation: The authors admit that the lines are artificial and insist that they are needed. (2) keeps only the admission, (3) takes the lines literally, and (4) reverses their argument about readability.

items.stem: Some researchers of education claim that students learn from their mistakes only if they discover the mistakes by themselves, and only if they have an opportunity to correct them soon afterward. According to these researchers, a mistake that is marked by the teacher is quickly forgotten, since the student did not have to think about it, and a mistake that is discovered but not corrected leaves the student with a feeling of failure and nothing more. According to the view of these researchers, which of the following ways of returning a test is most likely to help students learn from their mistakes?
options: The teacher marks every mistake in red and returns the tests the next day
The teacher asks the students to find by themselves the mistakes in their tests, and returns to the material at the end of the year
The teacher writes on each test only how many mistakes it contains, and lets the students correct them during the same lesson
The teacher shows the class the most common mistake, explains it, and gives a new exercise the next day
items.explanation: Only (3) meets both conditions: the students find the mistakes themselves and correct them at once. (1) and (4) point out the mistakes, and (2) delays the correction.

items.stem: The following appeared in a book on family businesses: "The heir to a family business often feels that every decision he makes is being judged by the generations before him. He may attribute this feeling to his own lack of confidence, but in most cases it has a real basis. The founders' decisions, the promises made to long-serving employees and suppliers, and the family name on the sign all limit what he can do, even when he himself is not aware of them. A study of 120 such businesses found that fewer than a third of the heirs made a significant change in the first five years." Which of the following best summarizes the claim made in the text?
options: An heir who lacks confidence imagines that the previous generations are judging him
The heir should learn to identify which of the founders' decisions still bind him
Most heirs make no significant change in the first years because they are afraid of the previous generations
The heir's sense of being limited by the past of the business usually reflects real limits
items.explanation: The text says the feeling has a real basis and names its sources. (1) reduces it to lack of confidence, which the text rejects, (3) substitutes fear for real limits, and (2) is advice the text does not give.

items.stem: In paintings, films and children's books, Viking warriors often appear wearing helmets with horns. Yet the only complete Viking helmet that has been found, discovered in Norway in 1943, has no horns, and there is no evidence that Viking warriors wore horned helmets in battle. Horned helmets have indeed been found in Scandinavia, for example at Veksø in Denmark, but they date from about 900 BCE, some 1,700 years before the Viking age, and were apparently used in ceremonies. The image of the horned Viking spread mainly after the costume designer Carl Emil Doepler gave horned helmets to the characters in the first production of Wagner's Ring cycle in 1876. Which of the following claims does the text seek to refute?
options: In the first production of Wagner's Ring cycle some of the characters wore horned helmets
Horned helmets have been found in Scandinavia
Viking warriors wore helmets with horns
Horned helmets were used only in ceremonies
items.explanation: The text sets the popular picture against the evidence. (1) and (2) are stated as facts, not disputed, and (4) goes beyond the text's "apparently" about the Veksø helmets and is not the target.
facts: Only one reasonably complete Viking-age helmet is known: the Gjermundbu helmet, found in Norway in 1943; it has no horns
No contemporary evidence of horned Viking battle helmets
Veksø helmets (Denmark) date to about 900 BCE (Bronze Age), probably ceremonial
Carl Emil Doepler's costumes for the 1876 Bayreuth premiere of Der Ring des Nibelungen popularized horned helmets

items.stem: An international festival of amateur choirs has been held every summer since 1995 in a small town in the Alps. Each year up to twelve choirs take part, most of them from the host country, and the program is decided by a committee of three conductors. In 2019 four choirs from outside Europe took part, and although this is not a large number, it was the first time since 2011 that more than three choirs from outside Europe had taken part in the festival. Which of the following claims contradicts the information in the text?
options: In 2015 no choir from outside Europe took part in the festival
In 2005 five choirs from outside Europe took part
In 2013 exactly three choirs from outside Europe took part
In 2011 only two choirs from outside Europe took part
items.explanation: "The first time since 2011" means that in 2011 more than three choirs from outside Europe took part. (1) and (3) fit the years 2012-2018, and (2) concerns a year the text does not limit.

items.stem: The long-necked lute played today at village weddings in the mountains of Dalmeria developed, according to the music historian Professor Arnaud, from one of two older instruments. One is the "tarbek", a village instrument with frets, which are thin strips across the neck. The other is the "selim", an instrument once played at the royal court, which has a similar body but no frets. Frets allow a player to produce exactly the same notes every time, whereas on an instrument without frets the notes depend on the exact position of the finger. The village lute has eight frets. Which of the following claims can be inferred from the text?
options: The tarbek and the selim have an ability that the village lute does not have
Contrary to Arnaud's view, the village lute developed from an instrument of the royal court other than the selim
The tarbek and the village lute have an ability in common that the selim lacks
The village lute developed from the tarbek, since both instruments have frets
items.explanation: Frets make it possible to repeat exactly the same notes; the tarbek and the village lute have them and the selim does not. (1) reverses the grouping, (2) has no support, and (4) turns a shared feature into proof of descent, although Arnaud leaves both origins open.

items.stem: In 1978 the NASA scientist Donald Kessler warned that the growing number of objects in orbit around the earth could lead to a chain reaction. When two objects collide in orbit, they break into many fragments, each of which can hit other objects and break them as well. The more fragments there are, the greater the chance of further collisions, which produce still more fragments. In 2009 an American communications satellite and an old Russian satellite collided at a height of about 790 kilometers, producing about two thousand fragments large enough to be tracked from the ground. What is the main idea of the text?
options: Collisions between satellites are the main source of the objects that are in orbit around the earth
Collisions between objects in orbit create fragments, which in turn increase the chance of more collisions
The number of satellites launched each year has grown since 1978
Kessler's warning has already come true, and it is no longer safe to launch satellites
items.explanation: Kessler's point is the loop in which collisions make fragments and fragments make collisions. (1) overstates one link, (3) is not in the text, and (4) goes beyond the example of 2009.
facts: Donald J. Kessler (NASA) and Burton Cour-Palais, 1978, proposed the cascading collision scenario ('Kessler syndrome')
2009 collision of Iridium 33 and Kosmos-2251 at about 790 km altitude
It produced roughly 2,000 trackable fragments

items.stem: Edo, the city that is today Tokyo, was built mostly of wood and paper, and during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries it was struck by large fires every few years; in the fire of 1657 most of the city burned. Most merchants in Edo did not try to build houses that would not burn, since such houses were too expensive and the fires were too frequent. Instead, next to their houses they built storehouses called kura, with thick walls of earth covered with plaster, in which they kept their goods, account books and valuables. When a fire approached, they sealed the doors and windows of the kura with mud. According to the text, how did the kura reduce the damage that fires caused to the merchants?
options: The goods and records kept in them survived fires in which the houses burned
Their thick walls stopped fires from spreading from house to house
The merchants could live in the kura, which could not burn, instead of in their wooden houses
The kura replaced the wooden houses, which were too expensive to rebuild after every fire
items.explanation: The merchants did not protect their houses; they protected what they kept in the kura. (2) gives the kura a role the text does not give, and (3) and (4) contradict the kura being storehouses next to the houses.
facts: Edo (Tokyo) suffered frequent large fires; the Great Meireki Fire of 1657 destroyed most of the city
Merchants built kura (dozō) storehouses with thick earthen walls finished in plaster to protect goods and records
Doors and windows were sealed with mud/plaster when fire approached

items.stem: In 2018 the number of residents of a certain town who were treated for bee stings at its two clinics was twice as high as in 2017, and at one of the clinics a special hour was set aside for this every morning. The town's doctors believe that the reason is that there were more bees in the area in 2018, possibly because of the unusually warm spring. Which of the following provides a different explanation for the rise in the number of residents who were treated for bee stings?
options: Until 2018 many of the town's residents were treated at a clinic in the neighboring town, which closed that year
Most people who are stung by bees are not allergic to the sting
In 2018 the council hired a beekeeper to remove hives from the public gardens and from the schoolyards
In 2018 fewer residents than usual spent time in the orchards around the town
items.explanation: If people who used to be treated elsewhere now came to the town's clinics, the count rises with no change in stings. (3) and (4) point to fewer stings, and (2) says nothing about the change.

items.stem: Around the year 1000, a small cave among the Mogao caves near Dunhuang, in western China, was sealed. It contained tens of thousands of manuscripts, paintings and printed texts in Chinese, Tibetan and other languages. The cave was discovered in 1900 by a Taoist monk, Wang Yuanlu. Among its contents was a copy of the Diamond Sutra printed in 868, the oldest printed book that bears a date. In 1907 the explorer Aurel Stein bought thousands of the manuscripts from Wang, and in the following years other expeditions took more, so that today the contents of the cave are divided mainly among libraries in London, Paris, Beijing and St. Petersburg. Which of the following titles best suits the text?
options: The Diamond Sutra - the oldest dated printed book
The library cave of Dunhuang - from a sealed cave to libraries around the world
The monasteries of western China and the languages of their manuscripts
Aurel Stein and the dispute over the manuscripts of Dunhuang
items.explanation: The text follows the cave's contents from their sealing to their present dispersal. (1) is one item, (3) is background, and (4) names a dispute the text does not describe.
facts: Mogao Cave 17 ('Library Cave') near Dunhuang was sealed around the early 11th century
Discovered in 1900 by the Taoist monk Wang Yuanlu
Contained tens of thousands of documents in Chinese, Tibetan and other languages
Includes the Diamond Sutra printed in 868, the oldest dated printed book
Aurel Stein acquired thousands in 1907; Pelliot and others followed; now in London, Paris, Beijing, St. Petersburg

items.stem: William Morris, the English designer and poet, believed that the industrial production of the nineteenth century had filled homes with ugly objects and had turned workers into servants of machines. In 1861 he founded, with several friends, a company that produced furniture, wallpaper, fabrics and stained glass by hand, in the manner of medieval craftsmen, and he hoped that such work would restore to workers their pleasure in their labor. Handmade objects, however, were expensive, and most of the company's customers were wealthy. Morris, who later became an active socialist, complained that he spent his life serving the luxury of the rich. Which of the following is implied by the text?
options: After his company succeeded, Morris gave up his socialist views
Objects made by hand, like those of Morris's company, are more beautiful than objects made by machines in factories
Had Morris used machines, his products would have reached the workers
Although Morris opposed the society of his time, his products served mainly those who benefited most from it
items.explanation: Morris set out against industrial society, yet his costly handmade goods went mainly to the wealthy. (1) contradicts his later socialism, (2) is Morris's view, not something the text asserts, and (3) is a counterfactual the text does not support.
facts: William Morris (1834-1896), English designer and poet, critic of industrial production
Founded Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co. in 1861, producing furniture, wallpaper, textiles and stained glass by hand
Handmade goods were expensive; customers were largely wealthy
Morris became an active socialist in the 1880s and lamented 'ministering to the swinish luxury of the rich' (paraphrased)

items.stem: The following appeared in an article on bird research: "Some ornithologists refuse to use counts made by amateur birdwatchers, and the reason they give is that amateurs misidentify species. It is true that amateurs make more mistakes than professionals. But the size of their mistakes can be measured, for example by sending experts to count alongside them, and taken into account. Without the amateurs we would have almost nothing: the Christmas Bird Count, which has been held in North America every year since 1900, now includes tens of thousands of volunteers." The author of the article seeks to refute a certain claim. Which of the following is it most likely to be?
options: Because amateurs make mistakes, their counts should not be used in research
Amateur birdwatchers make more mistakes in identifying species than professionals do
A large quantity of data is more important than accurate data
The Christmas Bird Count has been held every year since 1900
items.explanation: The author answers those who reject amateur counts because of their mistakes. (2) is a point the author grants, (4) is a fact the author cites, and (3) is a claim the author does not make.
facts: The Christmas Bird Count, organized by the National Audubon Society, has been held annually since 1900 (Frank Chapman)
It now involves tens of thousands of volunteers

items.stem: Sandy Island, a small island in the Coral Sea between Australia and New Caledonia, appeared on nautical charts from the late nineteenth century onward, and later also on world atlases and on Google Earth. In 2012 an Australian research ship sailed to the place marked on the maps and found open sea, more than 1,000 meters deep. Historians of cartography note that such "phantom islands" could remain on maps for generations, because mapmakers copied from earlier maps, and because a mapmaker who removed an island that did exist could endanger ships, whereas keeping an island that did not exist seemed to cost nothing. According to the text, why could phantom islands remain on maps for a long time?
options: Because to mapmakers, removing an island that might exist seemed more dangerous than keeping one that might not
Because mapmakers did not know that earlier maps sometimes contained errors
Because ships that sailed near the places marked on the maps reported seeing the islands
Because mapmakers who copied from earlier maps worked less carefully than those who drew the originals
items.explanation: Mapmakers kept doubtful islands because the risks were unequal. (2) and (4) are not stated, and (3) contradicts the 2012 finding of open sea.
facts: Sandy Island (Coral Sea) appeared on charts from the late 19th century (reported by the whaler Velocity, 1876) and on Google Earth
In November 2012 the Australian research vessel RV Southern Surveyor found open ocean about 1,400 m deep at the location
Phantom islands persisted partly through copying and caution in removing hazards

items.stem: The astronomer Andrew Ellicott Douglass, the founder of the science of dating by tree rings, had by the 1920s built two separate sequences of rings. One went back year by year from the present, and the other was based on beams from ancient ruins in the southwestern United States and could not be tied to calendar years. In June 1929, at Show Low, Arizona, a team working for Douglass found a charred beam, later labeled HH-39, whose rings overlapped both sequences. Douglass was thus able to join them, and within a short time he dated the construction of Pueblo Bonito and dozens of other sites. Which of the following claims is not made in the text?
options: Before HH-39 was found, the ancient sequence could not be tied to calendar years
The beam HH-39 was found in Arizona
Douglass himself found the beam HH-39
HH-39 made it possible to date the construction of many ancient sites
items.explanation: The text says the beam was found by a team working for Douglass, not by Douglass himself. (1), (2) and (4) are each stated.
facts: A. E. Douglass, astronomer, founder of dendrochronology
By the 1920s he had a modern chronology and a 'floating' prehistoric chronology from Southwest ruins
Beam HH-39 was found on 22 June 1929 at Show Low, Arizona, by an expedition team (Lyndon Hargrave, Emil Haury)
It bridged the gap, allowing the dating of Pueblo Bonito and many other sites

items.stem: In a single hectare of rain forest in Ecuador, several hundred species of trees have been counted, whereas in a hectare of forest in Europe there are usually fewer than twenty. One explanation, proposed independently around 1970 by the ecologists Daniel Janzen and Joseph Connell, is that each species of tree has insects and fungi that specialize in attacking it. These pests are most common near the parent tree, so that its seedlings rarely survive close to it, and the space around it is left to seedlings of other species. According to this explanation, in temperate forests, where the effect is apparently weaker, a single species can cover large areas. The text was written in answer to a certain question. Which of the following is most likely to be that question?
options: Why do pests attack seedlings more than grown trees?
Why are there many more species of trees in a hectare of tropical forest than in a hectare of temperate forest?
How did Janzen and Connell come to propose the same explanation at about the same time, independently of each other?
Why do seedlings in tropical forests rarely survive near their parent tree?
items.explanation: The text begins with the difference between the two kinds of forest and gives an explanation for it. (4) asks about one step of the explanation only, (1) asks about something the text does not compare, and (3) is not addressed.
facts: Tropical plots in Ecuador (e.g. Yasuní) have several hundred tree species per hectare; European temperate forests typically fewer than twenty
Janzen-Connell hypothesis (Janzen 1970, Connell 1971): host-specific pests and pathogens near parent trees reduce conspecific seedling survival, promoting diversity
The effect is thought to be weaker in temperate forests

items.stem: The following appeared in a review of a new translation of a nineteenth-century Russian novel: "The translator has produced a Hebrew of rare richness; almost every sentence can be read aloud with pleasure, and the descriptions of the steppe are more beautiful here than in any earlier translation. The novel's heroes, however, are simple peasants, and in this translation they speak like professors of literature. The reader admires their sentences and no longer hears them." Which of the following best presents the reviewer's opinion of the translation?
options: The richness of its Hebrew makes up for the way the heroes speak
Its descriptions of the steppe are beautiful, but the rest of it is difficult to read aloud
Its language is admirable, but it does not suit the characters of the novel
It is better than the earlier translations, because the translator made the peasants speak like educated people
items.explanation: The reviewer praises the language and faults its fit to the characters. (1) weighs the two the wrong way, (2) takes back the praise, and (4) turns the fault into a merit.

items.stem: Gilad: "Two years ago the city closed the main street to cars, and since then the number of shops on it that have closed has fallen from about fifteen a year to four or five. But the residents of the side streets, where the cars now pass, complain of noise and traffic jams, and I am not sure that what the main street has gained, if the closing is really the reason for it, is worth what they have lost." Which of the following is not implied by Gilad's words?
options: Gilad does not dispute that fewer shops on the main street have closed
Before the change, fewer cars passed through the side streets
In Gilad's opinion, the situation of the shops is not the only thing that should be considered
Closing the main street to cars is what caused fewer shops on it to close
items.explanation: Gilad reports that fewer shops closed after the change, and he explicitly leaves open whether the closing is what helped them. (1), (2) and (3) follow from his words.

items.stem: For centuries the eruption of Vesuvius that buried Pompeii was dated to 24 August 79, on the basis of a letter by Pliny the Younger, whose manuscripts, however, give the date in several different forms. Some archaeologists had long pointed to autumn fruits found in the ruins. In 2018 an inscription in charcoal was found on a wall of a house that was being renovated at the time of the eruption. It bears a date equivalent to 17 October, and since charcoal writing fades quickly, it was probably written shortly before the eruption, in the year 79. According to the text, what role did the inscription play in dating the eruption?
options: It showed that the copyists of Pliny's letter, whose manuscripts give the date in several different forms, had made a mistake
It supplied a date after 24 August on which the house was still in use, and thus supported a later date for the eruption
It made it possible for the first time to read inscriptions in charcoal found in Pompeii
It proved that the eruption took place on 17 October
items.explanation: The inscription shows people at work in the house after 24 August, which points to a later eruption. (4) turns the date of the inscription into the date of the eruption, (1) goes beyond the text, and (3) is not mentioned.
facts: The traditional date 24 August 79 derives from Pliny the Younger's letter; manuscripts transmit variant dates
Autumn fruits and other finds suggested a later date
In 2018 a charcoal inscription in a house in Regio V (under renovation) was found, dated 'XVI K Nov' = 17 October
Charcoal writing is fragile, suggesting it was recent; many now place the eruption around 24 October 79

items.stem: When the American businessman Malcolm McLean sent the first shipment of goods in containers from Newark to Houston in 1956, the cost of loading fell from almost six dollars a ton to about sixteen cents, since whole containers were lifted onto the ship by crane instead of being loaded box by box. Within twenty years containers had become the standard method of shipping goods, and trade between countries grew. The change, however, was not good for everyone. Old ports that lacked space for cranes and container yards, such as the piers of Manhattan and Brooklyn, lost most of their traffic, and thousands of dockworkers, whose work was no longer needed, lost their jobs. Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the text?
options: Although shipping in containers made trade cheaper, some ports and workers lost because of it
Containers were meant to benefit all ports and workers equally, but in practice they benefited only the large ports
Since containers harmed dockworkers, they harmed trade between countries
The ports of Manhattan and Brooklyn lost their traffic because tens of thousands of dockworkers lost their jobs
items.explanation: The text sets a general benefit beside the losses of some. (2) supplies an aim the text does not mention, (3) contradicts the growth in trade, and (4) reverses cause and effect.
facts: Malcolm McLean's Ideal X sailed from Newark to Houston in 1956 with containers
Loading cost fell from about $5.86 per ton to about $0.16 (Marc Levinson, The Box)
Containerization became standard; old Manhattan and Brooklyn piers declined as Port Newark-Elizabeth grew; many longshoremen lost work

items.stem: The Great Elephant Census, whose results were published in 2016, was carried out from light aircraft that flew over eighteen African countries along fixed lines; the crews counted the elephants they saw on either side of the aircraft. The census found about 352,000 savanna elephants, and in the countries for which earlier figures existed their number had fallen by some 30 percent in seven years. The researchers noted that this number is probably lower than the true number, since elephants that stand under dense trees cannot be seen from the air, and some regions of the countries surveyed were not flown over at all. According to the text, why is the number found in the census probably lower than the true number?
options: Because elephants move from country to country, and the census covered only eighteen countries
Because some of the elephants that were seen may have been counted twice
Because some of the elephants in the countries surveyed were not seen by the crews
Because the census was carried out from aircraft and not on foot
items.explanation: Elephants under trees and in regions not flown over were missed. (2) would make the count too high, (4) describes the method without saying what it missed, and (1) concerns elephants outside the countries surveyed.
facts: Great Elephant Census (funded by Paul G. Allen), results published 2016
Aerial survey of 18 African countries
Counted about 352,000 savanna elephants; about 30% decline between 2007 and 2014
Aerial counts miss animals under canopy and in unsurveyed areas

items.stem: In 1935 about one hundred cane toads were brought from Hawaii to Queensland, in Australia, in order to eat the beetles that were damaging the sugar cane. The toads did not help: the beetles live high on the stalks of the cane, where the toads cannot reach them. The toads, however, found plenty of other food, bred quickly and spread over an area of more than a million square kilometers. Since their skin is poisonous, many of the native animals that eat them, such as certain snakes and lizards, die. According to the text, what is ironic about bringing the cane toads to Australia?
options: The toads ate the sugar cane instead of the beetles
The scientists who brought the toads had warned against releasing them
The beetles began to eat the young toads, and so their number grew
An animal brought in to fight a pest became a pest itself
items.explanation: The toad was meant to solve a pest problem and became one. (1), (2) and (3) are not stated.
facts: In 1935 about 100 (102) cane toads were brought from Hawaii to Queensland to control cane beetles
They failed; the beetles live high on the cane stalks
They spread over more than 1 million km2
Their toxins kill many native predators (e.g. quolls, some snakes and goannas)

items.stem: Many plants depend on outside help to carry their seeds away from the parent plant. The seeds of the maple have a kind of wing, and the wind can carry them tens of meters. The fruit of the coconut palm floats and can drift in the sea for weeks before it is washed ashore. Other seeds have hooks or bristles by which they cling to the fur of passing animals and are carried far away. Which of the following examples does not illustrate any of the ways mentioned in the text?
options: The seeds of the dandelion are carried away by the wind on a kind of small umbrella made of fine hairs
The burrs of the burdock stick to the coats of dogs and sheep and fall off far from the plant
The seeds of certain water lilies float on the water until they reach a new place
When the fruit of the squirting cucumber ripens, it bursts and throws its seeds several meters
items.explanation: The squirting cucumber disperses its seeds by its own force, a way the text does not mention. (1) is wind, (2) is animals' fur, and (3) is water.
facts: Maple samaras are wind-dispersed
Coconuts float and disperse by sea
Burrs with hooks (burdock) attach to animal fur
Dandelion pappus is wind-dispersed
Some water lily seeds float (hydrochory)
The squirting cucumber (Ecballium elaterium) ejects its seeds explosively when ripe

items.stem: According to Dr. Kreitz, who spent many years studying weddings in the villages of a certain region, during the twentieth century they changed from events of the whole village into events of the family. In the past every household contributed a dish, the tables were set up in the square, and anyone who passed by could sit down. At a wedding that Kreitz attended in 1978, the guests sat at tables with printed name cards, a cook from the city prepared the meal, and the band played songs that were on the radio at the time. The name cards on the tables at the wedding in 1978 are presented in the text as an example of -
options: the change of weddings from events of the village into events of the family
the influence of the city on village weddings
the contribution of every household to the wedding
the growing wealth of the villages in the twentieth century, which allowed families to hire a cook
items.explanation: Printed name cards mean a list of invited guests, not a meal open to anyone who passed by. (2) fits the cook and the band rather than the cards, (3) describes the past, and (4) is not in the text.

items.stem: Astronomers who study the center of the Milky Way cannot use ordinary telescopes, since between it and the earth lie huge clouds of dust that block visible light almost completely. They therefore use telescopes that detect infrared radiation and radio waves, which pass through the dust. In this way, for example, astronomers followed for more than twenty-five years the motion of stars around the black hole at the center of the galaxy, and in 2020 they received the Nobel Prize for this work. Based on the text, why can astronomers who study stars near the sun rely more on ordinary telescopes?
options: Because infrared telescopes cannot detect stars that are near the sun
Because the stars near the sun do not move around a black hole
Because between the earth and these stars there is usually not enough dust to block visible light
Because ordinary telescopes are more precise than telescopes that detect infrared radiation
items.explanation: Ordinary telescopes fail at the center only because of the dust; where there is no such dust, they can be used. (1), (2) and (4) supply reasons the text does not give.
facts: Dust in the galactic plane blocks visible light from the Galactic Center
Infrared and radio observations penetrate the dust
Reinhard Genzel's and Andrea Ghez's groups tracked stars around Sagittarius A* for over 25 years; Nobel Prize in Physics 2020

items.stem: The laws of Varnia distinguish between two kinds of old trees on private land: "planted" trees, which were planted by people, and "wild" trees, which grew by themselves. Trees of both kinds may be of the same species and of the same age, and in many cases it is hard to tell them apart. An owner who wishes to cut down a planted tree must obtain a permit from the municipality, which is usually granted, whereas a wild tree more than fifty years old may not be cut down at all. According to the text, which of the following questions must be answered in order to decide whether a sixty-year-old oak on private land in Varnia may be cut down at all?
options: Did the oak grow by itself, or was it planted?
Is the oak more than fifty years old?
Is the land on which the oak grows private land?
Has the owner of the land received a permit from the municipality?
items.explanation: Whether the tree may be cut down at all depends only on how it came to grow there. (2) and (3) are already settled, and a permit (4) matters only once it is known that the tree was planted.

items.stem: In a certain country a law was passed ten years ago that forbids local authorities to transfer their land to others except for the building of schools and clinics. Accordingly, the authorities may no longer sell land to private developers or exchange land with neighboring authorities. Moreover, in the past the authorities in most districts were allowed to lease land for up to ninety-nine years, whereas today they may not lease it at all. Since the law was passed, the number of new schools built each year has almost doubled. Which of the following sentences summarizes the text most accurately?
options: Before the law was passed, the authorities in most districts were allowed to lease their land
The land of local authorities may be transferred to others only for the building of schools and clinics
The law has almost doubled the number of new schools built each year
Since the law was passed, the authorities have hardly leased any land
items.explanation: Every provision described applies the one rule. (1) is a true detail but not a summary, (3) turns a sequence into a cause and is only a detail, and (4) softens "not at all" to "hardly".

items.stem: Dorit, the chair of the parents' committee, supported the plan to move the school to a new building on the edge of the city, although many parents opposed it because their children would have to travel by bus. She did not support the plan because she thought the opponents' concerns were unfounded. She supported it because the ministry had promised to build a science laboratory in the new building, and only there. In her view, as long as the laboratory is built, the travel is worth the trouble. Which of the following is most likely to cause Dorit to withdraw her support for the plan?
options: A letter from parents describing the difficulties of the daily bus ride
A notice from the ministry that the laboratory will be built in the old building as well
A decision to shorten the ride by adding a stop near the old building
A meeting with the principal at which she stresses how hard the travel will be for young children
items.explanation: Dorit's only reason for the move is the laboratory; if it comes to the old building anyway, the reason disappears. (1) and (4) tell her what she already accepts, and (3) makes the plan easier to support.

items.stem: In 1982 a Turkish sponge diver reported seeing "metal biscuits with ears" on the seabed near Uluburun, on the southern coast of Turkey. They turned out to be copper ingots from a ship that sank at the end of the fourteenth century BCE. During eleven seasons of excavation, archaeologists raised about ten tons of copper and about one ton of tin - roughly the proportions needed to make bronze - as well as glass, ivory, spices and jewelry from at least seven different cultures. Which of the following claims is made in the text?
options: The ship sank on its way to Egypt
The wreck was discovered in 1982 by archaeologists who were searching for ancient ships off the coast of Turkey
The ratio between the copper and the tin in the cargo is close to the ratio used to make bronze
Most of the cargo was produced in Anatolia
items.explanation: The text states that the quantities of copper and tin were roughly the proportions needed for bronze. (2) is contradicted, since a sponge diver found the wreck, and (1) and (4) are not stated.
facts: The Uluburun wreck, off southern Turkey, was reported in 1982 by sponge diver Mehmed Çakır, who described 'metal biscuits with ears' (oxhide ingots)
Dated to the late 14th century BCE
Excavated 1984-1994 (eleven campaigns) by the Institute of Nautical Archaeology (George Bass, Cemal Pulak)
About 10 tons of copper and 1 ton of tin (the 10:1 ratio for bronze), plus glass, ivory, spices and jewelry from at least seven cultures

items.stem: A new book on the history of the newspapers of a certain country opens with the first weekly, which appeared in 1850 and was printed by hand, and ends with the closing of the last evening paper in 2004. Most of its chapters, however, are devoted to the fifteen years after the introduction of the rotary press in 1905, a period that the author calls "the years of the dailies". According to the text, in which period, in the author's view, was the country's press at its height?
options: After the last evening paper closed
Before newspapers were printed on rotary presses
In the fifteen years before 1905
In the fifteen years after 1905
items.explanation: A history of the press that dwells on "the years of the dailies" places its height there. (1) and (2) are where the book ends and begins, and (3) is the period before the one it dwells on.

items.stem: In 1976 the Hōkūle'a, a double-hulled sailing canoe built on the model of ancient Polynesian canoes, sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti, a distance of about 4,000 kilometers, without a compass or any other instrument. Its navigator, Mau Piailug, from the island of Satawal in Micronesia, found the way by the stars, the swells and the flight of birds. The voyage was planned by researchers who rejected the view, held by some scholars at the time, that the islands of Polynesia had been settled by people whose canoes drifted there by chance. What was the purpose of the voyage, according to the text?
options: To show that the islands of Polynesia could have been settled by planned voyages
To test whether a canoe built on the ancient model could survive a long voyage at sea
To find the route by which the first settlers reached Hawaii from Tahiti
To show that navigators from Micronesia could find their way better than navigators from Polynesia
items.explanation: The voyage was planned to answer the theory of accidental drift. (2) is at most a means, (3) is not stated, and (4) is not a comparison the text makes.
facts: Hōkūle'a, a double-hulled voyaging canoe (Polynesian Voyaging Society), sailed Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976, about 4,000 km
Navigator Mau Piailug of Satawal (Micronesia) used traditional non-instrument wayfinding (stars, swells, birds)
The project (Ben Finney and others) aimed to refute Andrew Sharp's accidental-drift theory of Polynesian settlement

items.stem: In July 1983 an Air Canada Boeing 767 ran out of fuel at a height of about 12,000 meters, on a flight from Montreal to Edmonton. The airline had just begun to measure fuel in kilograms instead of pounds, and since the fuel gauges were not working, the ground crew calculated the amount of fuel by hand. They converted liters of fuel into weight using the number 1.77, the weight in pounds of one liter of fuel, as though it were the weight in kilograms. As a result the plane took off with less than half the fuel it needed. The pilots managed to glide to a former air force base at Gimli, and no one was killed. According to the text, why did the crew believe that the plane had enough fuel?
options: Because a figure that referred to pounds was used as if it referred to kilograms
Because the new plane measured fuel in liters and not in kilograms
Because the fuel gauges, which were not working properly, showed a larger amount of fuel than there was
Because a kilogram of fuel weighs less than a pound of fuel
items.explanation: The crew used the right number with the wrong unit. (3) contradicts the gauges not working, (4) reverses the units, and (2) describes a step, not the error.
facts: Air Canada Flight 143, Boeing 767, 23 July 1983, Montreal-Edmonton (via Ottawa)
Ran out of fuel at about 41,000 ft (~12,500 m)
Fuel quantity indicators were inoperative; manual calculation used 1.77 (lb per liter) instead of 0.8 (kg per liter) during the metric changeover
The aircraft had less than half the required fuel; it glided to the former RCAF Station Gimli; no fatalities

items.stem: The following appeared in a report on the dairy industry of a certain country: "The number of dairy farms in the northern district fell steadily between 1970 and 1990, hardly changed during the 1990s, and rose in the first decade of the 2000s, until it passed its 1970 level. The trend in the district is similar to the trend in the country as a whole, but in the country as a whole the rise in the 2000s was sharper, so that the difference between the number of farms in 2010 and the number in 1970 was greater than in the district." Based on the above, which of the following claims is definitely true?
options: The number of dairy farms in the northern district rose in every year of the first decade of the 2000s
In the 1990s the number of dairy farms in the country as a whole hardly changed
The fall between 1970 and 1990 was steeper in the country as a whole than in the district
In 2010 there were more dairy farms in the country as a whole than in 1970
items.explanation: The district ended above its 1970 level, and the country's gain was larger still, so the country too ended above 1970. (1) turns an overall rise into a rise every year, (2) turns "similar" into "the same", and (3) is not given.

items.stem: The following appeared in an article on the teaching of mathematics: "But the fact that the textbook has been used in the country's schools for forty years does not prove that it is a good textbook. Teachers tend to prefer the book from which they themselves learned, and publishers are in no hurry to replace a book that sells. Anyone who wishes to judge the textbook fairly must read it as if he had never seen it before." Which of the following sentences most likely came just before this excerpt?
options: The textbook is used in almost all the schools of the country, but it may be that this is nothing more than habit.
The textbook was first published forty years ago, and since then it has been revised three times, the last time in 2010.
The textbook has been in use for forty years, and its supporters regard this as proof of its quality.
The teachers who use the textbook are divided on the question of whether it is a good book.
items.explanation: The excerpt's "But" answers the claim that forty years of use prove the book's quality. (1) already contains the excerpt's doubt, (4) does not mention the long use, and (2) gives the "But" nothing to answer.

items.stem: The Empire State Building in New York is struck by lightning more than twenty times a year on average, and the park ranger Roy Sullivan was struck seven times between 1942 and 1977 and survived all of them. Lightning tends to strike the highest point in its area, so that tall buildings, lone trees and people standing in open fields are struck again and again. The popular saying about lightning is therefore mistaken. According to the text, what does the popular saying claim?
options: Lightning tends to strike the highest point in its area
A place that has been struck by lightning will not be struck again
Tall buildings are struck by lightning more often than people
Lightning does not strike buildings that are protected by lightning rods
items.explanation: The examples of repeated strikes answer the belief that lightning does not strike the same place twice. (1) is the text's own explanation, (3) is a comparison the text does not make, and (4) is not addressed.
facts: The Empire State Building is struck by lightning about 20-25 times a year (NWS: about 23)
Roy Sullivan, a U.S. park ranger, was struck seven times between 1942 and 1977 (Guinness record) and survived
Lightning tends to strike tall, isolated objects
Popular saying: 'lightning never strikes the same place twice'
